summary: One of a series of surveys by David Smallberg checking which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP. This edition tested hosts in December 1982. Replaced by RFC 834.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on the door of every computer on the list to see which ones answered. This is the result for one week.

questions: which hosts accepted telnet in december 1982
what is the nic host table
subtitle: A weekly survey of which ARPANET hosts actually answered Telnet, FTP and SMTP connection attempts over TCP.

tldr.problem: People wanted to know which hosts listed in the NIC host table really accepted TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and mail, not just which ones claimed to.
tldr.mechanism: David Smallberg tried connections to every host on the list (314 hosts) and published summary tables plus a per-host result for each of the three services.
tldr.outcome: RFC 833 is one weekly snapshot, tested The tests were run on 14-Dec-82 from about 8:00 am to about 4:30 pm PST.. It is superseded by RFC 834, the next report in the series.

today: RFC 833 is obsoleted by RFC 834, the next report in the series, and its figures are a snapshot from December 1982.

sections.title: What Was Tested and When
sections.content:
RFC 833 is a survey, not a protocol. Its list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 2-Dec-82. The tests were run on 14-Dec-82 from about 8:00 am to about 4:30 pm PST. Hosts that were dead, refused or unreachable were tried again on 14-Dec-82 from about 10:15 pm to about 11:45 pm PST.

The RFC notes that duplicately listed hosts were removed slightly differently from the previous week's report, so the row totals in the summary tables are slightly changed from last week.

The question is practical: of the hosts that claim to support a service in the NIC table, and of those that claim nothing, which ones really accept a TCP connection for Telnet, FTP and SMTP?
sections.eli5: It is like checking a list of shops to see which ones are really open, instead of trusting the sign on the door.

sections.title: Claims and Results
sections.content:
Each host's claims come from the NIC host table and are shown as four letters: T for tcp with no particular services mentioned, t for tcp/telnet, f for tcp/ftp and s for tcp/smtp.

The results for each service are one of: blank (not accepted), refused, unreachable, dead, accepted, or accepted+. The last means FTP allowed user anonymous with password guest.
sections.eli5: The claim is what a host says about itself. The result is what happened when someone actually knocked.

sections.title: The Summary Tables
sections.content:
There is one summary table per service. Rows split the hosts by what they claimed (tcp/telnet, tcp, or nothing), and columns by result. All three tables cover the same 314 hosts.

  • Telnet: 103 hosts accepted a connection. Of the 130 hosts claiming tcp/telnet, 77 accepted.
  • FTP: 90 hosts accepted or accepted+. Of the 107 claiming tcp/ftp, 60 did.
  • SMTP: 82 hosts accepted. Of the 96 claiming tcp/smtp, 57 did.

Some hosts that claimed nothing in the NIC table still accepted connections, and some that claimed a service were dead or unreachable, so the claims are only a rough guide.
sections.eli5: The tables count how many doors opened, how many stayed shut and how many houses nobody could find.

sections.title: The Per-Host Listing
sections.content: The rest of the RFC is a table in alphabetical order by host name. Each row gives the host name, its address (for example 10.2.0.54), its claims, and its Telnet, FTP and SMTP results. A blank result means the service was not accepted. Some rows show d e a d or u n r e a c h a b l e spread across the columns. The listing ends with hosts such as ndre1, which accepted all three services with FTP marked accepted+, and two clarksburg hosts that were unreachable.
sections.eli5: After the counts comes the full guest book: one line per computer saying what happened when it was knocked on.

sections.title: Place in the Series
sections.content: This is one report in a series of surveys by the same author. It supersedes the earlier report, RFC 832. The metadata lists RFC 834 as the report that obsoletes it. Because it records one test run, its figures describe a few days in December 1982 and nothing more.
sections.eli5: It is one photograph of the network on one day, and a newer photograph replaced it.
